stops.name: Mount Etna, the fada de Gibel
stops.campa: In the Occitan romance of Jaufre, composed for the courts of Aragon within a generation or two of Chrétien, Morgan's name has already crossed the sea and taken a mountain: she appears as the fada de Gibel, the Fairy of Gibel, Gibel being the Arabic name the Sicilians themselves give Mount Etna. No valley in Brittany holds her now; a whole volcano does, its fire read as her hearth and her power, its height as her tower over the strait. The Bretons who came to Sicily in the wake of the Norman conquest brought Arthur and his sister with them, and the mountain kept them both.

stops.name: Mount Etna, the bishop's horse and the groom
stops.campa: Gervase of Tilbury, writing for the Emperor Otto IV, records a stranger tale still: a bishop of Catania loses his finest horse up the mountain's slopes, and the groom who chases it past the crater's lip finds himself led by an old man through smoke into a hall where Arthur himself sits enthroned, nursing the wound Mordred gave him, breaking open fresh each year. Arthur has the horse fetched and returned, sends the bishop a gift and a warning against his cruelty, and lets the groom go home to tell it. The mountain the Sicilians call Mongibel keeps a king as well as a queen, brother and sister ruling the same dark court under the same fire.

stops.name: Wolframs-Eschenbach, Terdelaschoye of Feimurgân
stops.campa: At his desk in Bavaria, Wolfram von Eschenbach performs the last fold. He tells of Mazadan, a mortal king whom a fay claimed for her love: Terdelaschoye they called her, and she led him away to Feimurgân. The names have changed places. Terre de la Joie, the Land of Joy, has become a woman; Fee Morgân, Morgan the fairy, has become a country, and elsewhere in the poem it is a mountain, Fay Morgan's mystic mount, as though the poet already knew about Etna. Through their sons the line runs down to Parzival and Anjou. She began as a woman with a mother and a birthplace. She ends as a place.
stops.quote: And Mazadan was their father whom a fay for her love did claim. Terre-de-la-schoie did they call her, to Fay-Morgan she led the king.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book I, tr. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
